analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal income tax code after 2001, naming no replacement tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the federal income tax code after 2001 drew 38 Senate Republicans as sponsors or cosponsors but never received a Finance Committee action or any floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have terminated the entire Internal Revenue Code — the federal income, estate, gift, and excise taxes — for everything after December 31, 2001. It kept only the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. It did not create a replacement tax; it simply declared that Congress should approve a new 'simple and fair' system by July 4, 2001. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed as written, everyone who owes federal income tax would stop paying it after 2001 — with the largest dollar savings going to high earners, investors, and large estates, since those groups pay the most income and estate tax. Advocates of a flat tax or national sales tax would also gain, because the bill forces a rewrite of the tax system with no specified design.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Internal Revenue Code from imposing any tax for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2001, ending the federal income, estate, gift, and excise taxes.
Exempts from termination the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare (self-employment tax, FICA, and the Railroad Retirement tax), so those programs' dedicated funding continues.

Declares that any replacement system should apply a low rate to all Americans, relieve working Americans, protect taxpayer rights, remove the bias against saving and investment, promote growth and jobs, and not penalize marriage or families.

analysis.who_pays: The bill names no replacement, so the cost would fall on whatever Congress enacted afterward — or, if nothing was enacted in time, on every federal program funded by the income tax. A national sales tax, the most commonly discussed replacement, collects the same revenue from spending rather than income, which weighs relatively heavier on lower-income households who spend most of what they earn. Meanwhile Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes would continue unchanged, so the tax burden on working paychecks would not disappear.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unspecified — future taxpayers and federal programs

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no replacement tax system; it only 'declares' that Congress should approve a new one by July 4, 2001, so enacting it alone would cut off most federal revenue with nothing scheduled to take its place.

With income, estate, gift, and excise taxes gone but Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes retained, the remaining payroll taxes would continue to fund only those programs — leaving defense, highways, education, and everything else the income tax pays for without funding unless a replacement passed in time.

Because the bill leaves the replacement open, the new system could be a consumption-based tax, which collects from what people spend rather than what they earn and falls proportionally harder on households with lower incomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promises a simpler, fairer tax system but delivers no actual replacement — only a sunset date and a set of aspirations. Enacted as written, it would have created a revenue cliff that either forced deep cuts to federal programs or an eleventh-hour tax rewrite of unknown design, most plausibly a consumption tax whose burden falls harder on ordinary households than the progressive income tax it would replace. Its practical function was as a statement of position rather than a workable law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 1998, by Senator Tim Hutchinson with 26 original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The bill attracted 37 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, in addition to the Republican sponsor.
After the referral to Finance, no further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyone who depends on federal programs paid for by the income tax — from defense to highways to education — was spared a bill that would have ended that funding with no replacement in place. Opponents of shifting the tax burden onto consumption were also better off that it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Programs funded by the income tax

for.name: Sen. Tim Hutchinson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 37 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican, including Majority Leader Trent Lott and Budget Committee Chair Pete Domenici among the original cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. William Roth
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 senators behind the bill — the sponsor and all 37 cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it; the referral to the Finance Committee was the bill's last recorded action.

industries.note: Ending the progressive income tax and the estate and gift taxes with no replacement would deliver the largest dollar savings to the highest earners and biggest estates. Meanwhile the payroll taxes funding Social Security and Medicare would continue, keeping the tax on wages intact.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Its revenue depends on the complexity of the income tax code the bill would terminate. Whether taxpayers were actually better off would depend entirely on what, if anything, replaced it.

industries.industry: Advocates of a flat tax or national retail sales tax
industries.note: By sunsetting the current code without naming a successor, the bill forces a rewrite of the tax system on their preferred terms. A consumption-based replacement would shift more of the tax burden onto everyday spending.
